chunks: From him, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, from Ali ibn al-Hazwar, from al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah, who said:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), when he raised his head from prostration, would sit until he was at ease, then he would stand. He was asked, 'O Commander of the Faithful, before you, Abu Bakr and Umar, when they raised their heads from prostration, would rise on the balls of their feet as a camel rises.' The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said, 'Only the stiff/hasty people of the people do that. Indeed, this is from the reverence of prayer.'
ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali rise from prostration compared to Abu Bakr and Umar?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights Imam Ali’s (AS) emphasis on *tawqir* (reverence and dignity) in prayer, contrasting his composed, seated rise from prostration with the brisk, camel-like motion attributed to the early Caliphs, which he characterized as *jafa'* (stiffness or haste). This distinction underscores the Shia scholarly view that the physical demeanor of prayer reflects inner spiritual presence (*khushu*), prioritizing solemnity over mere mechanical speed. The hadith serves as a foundational text for the jurisprudential preference of sitting briefly after prostration to ensure physical and mental composure before resuming the next position.
